anchorClaim: Individuals with eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or clinical risk populations) show measurable structural or functional brain differences, in regions associated with emotion processing and cognitive control, detectable via MRI or fMRI compared to healthy controls.
dataQualityNote: This pull is a real 91-datom evidence set, but it has notable quality flags worth surfacing: 44 of 91 datoms (48%) are marked theme_match_low_confidence by the platform's own matching pipeline, and inspection shows several of these are only tangentially related to the anchor claim (e.g. EEG mind-wandering in shift workers, fMRI social-learning tasks in healthy adults, object-recognition memory in rats) rather than direct eating-disorder neuroimaging evidence. Evidence-type metadata is also thin: 40 of 91 datoms (44%) are evidence_type TEXT_NO_METADATA rather than PDF_FULL_TEXT, and 24 of 91 datoms have sample_size "Not reported." Methodology is highly heterogeneous (72 distinct methodology strings across 91 datoms, mostly singletons), which limits direct study-design comparison. No malformed records were skipped; all 91 datom_ids referenced by the Datomer record were successfully fetched.

guide.whatScienceSays: Of the 91 real datoms linked to this claim, 64 (70%) directly support measurable structural or functional brain differences in people with eating disorders, most commonly reduced gray matter volume, altered cortical thickness, and disrupted resting-state or task-based functional connectivity in regions tied to emotion processing and cognitive control (insula, orbitofrontal cortex, amygdala-prefrontal circuits). 25 datoms (27%) are conditional, often narrowing the effect to a subgroup, a specific region, or a BMI-linked association rather than a clean case-control difference. Only 2 datoms (2%) contradict the claim outright, one a population-based adolescent cohort finding no significant global brain-volume association with subclinical binge-eating symptoms, the other an animal (rat) behavioral study not measuring brain structure directly.
guide.howConfident: The platform scores this claim's confidence_band as Preliminary at 35%, despite 91 replications, and that caution is warranted by real data-quality patterns in the fetched set: 44 of 91 datoms (48%) are flagged theme_match_low_confidence by the platform's own matching pipeline, and several of these describe populations or outcomes only loosely related to eating disorders (shift-worker EEG studies, healthy-adult social-learning fMRI, ADHD cortical-thickness studies, rat object-recognition memory). Evidence-type metadata is also thin, with 40 of 91 datoms (44%) sourced as TEXT_NO_METADATA rather than full-text PDFs, and 24 of 91 datoms missing a reported sample size. Methodology is fragmented across 72 distinct descriptions for 91 datoms, limiting direct comparability of study designs.
decisionSupport: The directional signal (70% supports, 2% contradicts) is consistent with a real, measurable brain-structure and brain-function difference in eating disorders, most concentrated in insula, prefrontal, and connectivity measures.

Treat this as preliminary rather than clinically established: the platform's own confidence_band is 'Preliminary,' and nearly half the underlying datoms have low thematic-match confidence to the anchor claim.

Findings vary by eating-disorder subtype (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating) and by measure (volume vs. connectivity vs. cortical thickness), so this should not be read as one uniform brain signature.
Before treating this as decision-grade evidence, a manual review to strip out the ~44 low-confidence-match datoms would materially change both the effective sample size and the apparent consensus.
guide.faultLines: Nearly half the fetched datoms (44 of 91) are flagged as having low thematic-match confidence to the anchor claim, and manual inspection confirms some describe unrelated populations (shift workers, rats, ADHD patients, healthy adults in social-learning tasks) rather than eating-disorder patients specifically. Sample-size reporting is inconsistent, with 24 of 91 datoms lacking a stated sample size, and most studies are cross-sectional, limiting causal inference about whether brain differences precede or result from disordered eating.

name: Structural Brain Alterations in Eating Disorders
plainQuestion: Do brain scans (MRI/fMRI) show measurable structural or functional differences in people with eating disorders compared to people without them?
